title: How to Secure Your Home Before Going on Vacation
excerpt: Leave for vacation with your home prepared: camera checks, lived-in signals, mail and social habits, and a remote routine while you are away.
author: HiddenCameras Editorial Team
authorBio: The HiddenCameras.tv editorial team researches and writes about security cameras, surveillance technology, and home safety.
body:
An empty house tells on itself: stacked parcels, unchanging lights, a silent driveway at the same hours daily. Securing your home before vacation means breaking those patterns so the house looks lived in, keeping cameras and alerts monitored from afar, and lining up one person who can stand in your driveway if something looks wrong.

Work in three passes: setup a week before, checks the night before and the morning you leave, and a light remote routine that keeps you informed without ruining the trip. Each takes under an hour.

A week out: make the house look stubbornly normal

  1. Stop the pile-ups. Pause mail and parcels or route them to a neighbor. Nothing advertises absence like a stuffed mailbox and boxes on the step.
  2. Vary the light. Put two or three lamps on staggered timers, set for hours you actually use them. A bedroom lamp that clicks off at your usual bedtime sells occupancy better than a floodlight burning all night.
  3. Quiet the bins and the lawn. Ask someone to bring bins in on collection day and keep the yard roughly as you would. An untouched lawn for two weeks is a calendar of your absence.
  4. Go silent about dates. Do not post itineraries or countdowns publicly. Save photos for after you are home, and keep travel confirmations off shared calendars.

Walk the street side with fresh eyes and fix whatever screams empty: the spare key under the planter, which should move indoors now, and the upstairs window latched open.

Set cameras to watch the right things while you are gone

Vacation changes what cameras are for. Normally they deter and document; while you travel they must also summon help, which means alerts have to reach you and footage has to survive a break-in. Confirm remote viewing works on mobile data by testing from down the street, and check that storage has room for the whole trip plus a margin.

Re-aim with absence in mind. The doorbell view should include the parcel drop zone, the driveway camera should show whether a car is present, and one indoor camera in a main living area can confirm whether movement is a person or a curtain. If indoor cameras are normally off, decide whether one stays on, tell any housesitter in writing, and face it at entries.

The night-before camera pass that catches dead zones

After dark, walk each camera's view as a visitor would approach and confirm your face is visible, not silhouetted. Trigger motion at each camera and verify the alert arrives within a minute. Check batteries, wipe lenses, and confirm time stamps. Anything that fails gets fixed or covered by a neighbor check, not wished well.

Lock, shut off, and unplug the unglamorous stuff

Work room by room on the last evening. Lock every window and test each one by pushing, since latched-looking handles often miss the catch. Deadbolt exterior doors and confirm the garage door is fully closed from inside. Shut off water valves to washing machines and consider the main supply if nobody will be home; a burst hose does more damage in ten empty days than a break-in.

Unplug small heat-producing appliances and clear perishables from the refrigerator. Set an away temperature that protects pipes without paying to comfort an empty house. Leave one car in the driveway if possible and take the garage remote with you.

Give one trusted person the keys and the playbook

No camera calls a neighbor. Choose one nearby person, hand over a key in person, and write down the essentials: your return date, alarm and camera basics, shutoff and breaker locations, and permission to enter if an alert fires. Show them a normal alert versus the siren-level one.

Agree on visible signs of life: parking in your drive once or twice, adjusting blinds, putting a bin out. Offer the same when they travel. Reciprocal arrangements get kept; one-sided favors get forgotten.

Lock down the digital trail before you board

Update camera and router firmware while you still have time to recover from a glitch, then confirm each device is back online. Turn on login alerts, use unique passwords with two-factor authentication, and remove old shared users such as a former housesitter.

Silence non-essential notifications into a trip profile so genuine alerts still break through. A phone buzzing at every passing cat on day one gets muted by day three, exactly when the real alert arrives.

What to do if an alert fires from a thousand miles away

Decide the order now while calm: check the live clip, call your key-holder with a specific request, and only then consider authorities. Send the clip, the camera name, and what you want done: please drive past, check the back gate, call me back within ten minutes. Save home-area non-emergency numbers in your phone before departure.

Come home to a house that kept its secrets

On return, walk the perimeter first, checking for forced windows, moved items, and water stains on ceilings. Review saved clips for anything dismissed mid-trip, then return timers, thermostats, and camera privacy settings to normal.

Close the loop with your key-holder and your future self: note which camera missed what and which timer looked fake. That five-minute debrief is what turns this year's decent setup into next year's secure one.
